items.title: Regions & Availability Zones
items.context: A region is a geographic area (eu-west-3 is Paris) made of several Availability Zones: physically separate data centres with independent power and networking. Spreading instances across AZs survives a data-centre failure.

questions.prompt: To survive one data centre going down, deploy across:
questions.explanation: Load balancers and RDS Multi-AZ are built around this.

items.title: IAM roles
items.context: IAM users are long-lived identities; roles are assumed and give temporary credentials. EC2 instances, Lambda functions and CI pipelines should use roles (instance profiles, execution roles, OIDC federation) rather than stored access keys. Grant least privilege.

questions.prompt: An EC2 app needs to read one S3 bucket. Best practice:
choices: Attach an IAM role with read access to that bucket
Put an admin user's access keys in the app config
questions.explanation: The SDK picks up the role's temporary credentials automatically.

items.title: Policy evaluation
items.context: Requests are denied by default. An explicit Allow grants access, but an explicit Deny in any applicable policy always overrides an Allow.

questions.prompt: One policy allows s3:* and another explicitly denies s3:DeleteObject. Deleting an object is:
choices: Allowed only for the root user
Denied — an explicit deny always wins
Decided by whichever policy is newer
questions.explanation: This is how service control policies and permission boundaries set guardrails.

items.title: VPC subnets
items.context: A public subnet has a route to an Internet Gateway. A private subnet doesn't; its instances reach the internet outbound through a NAT Gateway in a public subnet. Databases and app servers usually live in private subnets behind a load balancer.

questions.prompt: Private-subnet instances need to download OS updates. They need:
choices: An Internet Gateway attached to the subnet
A NAT Gateway (in a public subnet) as their default route
questions.explanation: NAT allows outbound connections without accepting inbound ones.

items.title: Security groups vs NACLs
items.context: Security groups are stateful firewalls at the instance/ENI level: allow rules only, and return traffic is allowed automatically. Network ACLs are stateless filters at the subnet level with allow and deny rules, evaluated in order, so return traffic needs its own rule.

questions.prompt: Which is stateful, so return traffic is automatically allowed?
questions.explanation: With NACLs you must also open the ephemeral ports for responses.

items.title: Auto Scaling behind a load balancer
items.context: An Auto Scaling Group keeps a desired number of EC2 instances from a launch template, replaces unhealthy ones, and scales on metrics (e.g. target 50% CPU). An Application Load Balancer spreads traffic across them and health-checks them.

questions.prompt: Traffic doubles every evening. The cloud-native response is:
choices: Buy a bigger instance and keep it forever
An Auto Scaling Group with a target-tracking policy behind an ALB
questions.explanation: Scale out for the peak, back in afterwards, and pay for what you use.

items.title: S3
items.context: S3 is object storage designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability. Storage classes trade cost against access speed (Standard, Infrequent Access, Glacier). Versioning protects against overwrites and deletes; Block Public Access prevents accidental exposure.

questions.prompt: Which feature lets you recover an object someone overwrote by mistake?
questions.explanation: Lifecycle rules can expire old versions to control cost.

items.title: RDS Multi-AZ vs read replicas
items.context: RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ and fails over automatically — it's for availability; the standby doesn't serve reads (in the classic setup). Read replicas copy asynchronously and serve read traffic — they're for scaling reads.

questions.prompt: You need automatic failover if the primary database's AZ fails. Use:
choices: A read replica in the same AZ
questions.explanation: Add read replicas separately when reads, not availability, are the bottleneck.

items.title: Lambda
items.context: Lambda runs functions on demand with no servers to manage, billed per request and duration, scaling automatically. Limits to remember: a 15-minute maximum run time and cold-start latency when a new execution environment spins up.

questions.prompt: Which job is a poor fit for Lambda?
choices: A video encode that takes 2 hours
Resizing an image on upload to S3
A nightly cleanup script that runs for 30 s
questions.explanation: The 15-minute limit rules it out; use ECS/Fargate, Batch or EC2.

items.title: Shared responsibility
items.context: AWS secures the cloud itself (data centres, hardware, the virtualisation layer). You secure what you put in the cloud: IAM, data, network rules, OS patching on EC2, application code. The split shifts with the service: on Lambda AWS also patches the OS.

questions.prompt: On EC2, who patches the guest operating system?
questions.explanation: Managed services move more of that responsibility to AWS.

items.title: CloudWatch vs CloudTrail
items.context: CloudWatch collects metrics, logs and alarms: how resources behave. CloudTrail records API calls: who did what, when, from where — essential for audits and security investigations.

questions.prompt: Who deleted the production security group yesterday? Look in:
questions.explanation: CloudTrail logs every API call with the identity that made it.

items.title: EBS, EFS, S3
items.context: EBS is block storage attached to one EC2 instance in one AZ (like a disk). EFS is a managed NFS file system that many instances can mount across AZs. S3 is object storage accessed over HTTP APIs.

questions.prompt: Ten EC2 instances must share one POSIX file system. Use:
questions.explanation: EBS volumes attach to one instance at a time (multi-attach is a niche exception).

items.title: ECS/Fargate vs EKS
items.context: ECS is AWS's own container orchestrator; Fargate runs ECS (or EKS) tasks without managing servers. EKS is managed Kubernetes — portable and with a big ecosystem, but more to operate.

questions.prompt: A small team wants to run containers with the least operations work. Good default:
choices: Docker on one EC2 instance forever
questions.explanation: Pick EKS when you need Kubernetes itself.

items.title: Route 53 routing
items.context: Route 53 is AWS's DNS. Routing policies: simple, weighted (split traffic), latency-based (nearest region), failover (primary/secondary with health checks), geolocation. Alias records point at AWS resources, even at the zone apex.

questions.prompt: Send users to a standby region automatically if the primary fails health checks:
choices: A CNAME at the zone apex
questions.explanation: Health checks decide which record is answered.

items.title: CloudFront
items.context: CloudFront is AWS's CDN: it caches content at edge locations, terminates TLS near users and protects the origin (S3, ALB). Origin Access Control lets a private S3 bucket be read only through CloudFront.

questions.prompt: Serve a static site from a private S3 bucket over HTTPS worldwide:
choices: An EC2 web server per region
questions.explanation: The bucket stays private; only CloudFront can read it.

items.title: SQS vs SNS
items.context: SQS is a queue: messages wait until a consumer polls and deletes them (one consumer handles each message). SNS is pub/sub: a published message is pushed to every subscriber (SQS queues, Lambda, HTTP, email). A common pattern is SNS fan-out to several SQS queues.

questions.prompt: One 'order placed' event must reach billing, shipping and email services:
choices: A single SQS queue shared by all three
SNS fan-out (often into one SQS queue per service)
questions.explanation: With one shared queue, each message would go to only one of them.

items.title: DynamoDB keys
items.context: DynamoDB is a serverless key-value/document database. Every item has a partition key (and optionally a sort key); queries must target a partition key, and a high-cardinality, evenly used partition key avoids hot partitions.

questions.prompt: A poor partition key choice for a busy DynamoDB table is:
questions.explanation: Few distinct values concentrate traffic on a few partitions.

items.title: Spot instances
items.context: Spot instances use spare EC2 capacity at up to ~90% off, but AWS can reclaim them with a two-minute warning. They suit fault-tolerant, stateless or batch work — not a single critical database.

questions.prompt: Which workload fits Spot instances?
choices: A license server with one instance
Stateless CI runners or batch jobs that can be retried
questions.explanation: Mix Spot with On-Demand capacity in Auto Scaling Groups.

items.title: Commitment discounts
items.context: For steady, always-on usage, Savings Plans or Reserved Instances (1- or 3-year commitments) cut compute cost substantially compared with On-Demand prices.

questions.prompt: A service runs 24/7 at constant load for years. Cheapest sensible option:
choices: A Savings Plan or Reserved Instances
questions.explanation: Use On-Demand for spiky or uncertain workloads.

items.title: KMS
items.context: KMS manages encryption keys. Services like S3, EBS and RDS use KMS keys for encryption at rest; key policies and IAM control who can use them, and every use is logged in CloudTrail.

questions.prompt: What does KMS mainly provide?
choices: Managed encryption keys with access control and audit
questions.explanation: Use customer-managed keys when you need your own key policies or rotation control.

items.title: Well-Architected Framework
items.context: AWS's Well-Architected Framework reviews workloads against six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation and sustainability.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a Well-Architected pillar?
questions.explanation: The six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation, sustainability.
